section.title: SQLite3 vs Mongoose — Data Access Compared
section.subtitle: Raw SQL through Python's sqlite3 vs MongoDB access through the Mongoose ODM.

topics.title: What Each One Is
topics.learn: A SQL database driver vs a MongoDB ODM.

sqlite.definition: sqlite3 is Python's built-in driver for SQLite — a serverless, file-based relational database. You write SQL strings; tables have fixed schemas and relationships via keys.
sqlite.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('app.db')
cursor = conn.cursor()

# relational: tables + SQL + joins
cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > ?', (18,))

mongoose.definition: Mongoose is an ODM (Object-Document Mapper) for MongoDB — a document database storing flexible BSON/JSON-like documents. You define schemas in JS and query with a chainable API.

topics.title: Connecting to the Database
topics.learn: Opening a connection and preparing it.

sqlite.definition: sqlite3.connect() opens (or creates) a .db file — no server needed. Connections should be closed or used as context managers; row_factory gives dict-like rows.
sqlite.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('app.db')
conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row  # rows as dicts

cursor = conn.cursor()
cursor.execute('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)')
conn.commit()
conn.close()

mongoose.definition: mongoose.connect() opens a connection to a MongoDB server (local or Atlas cloud). Connection options set timeouts; models are compiled from schemas per collection.

sqlite.definition: Schema = CREATE TABLE with typed columns, constraints (PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY). SQLite is dynamically typed but column affinities hint types.
sqlite.code:
cursor.execute('''
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT UNIQUE,
  age INTEGER,
  created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
)
''')
conn.commit()

mongoose.definition: You define a Schema (fields, types, required, defaults, validators) then compile it into a Model — one model per collection. Schemas are flexible but enforce shape.

sqlite.definition: INSERT INTO with parameterised queries (?) prevents SQL injection — never format user input into SQL strings.
sqlite.code:
cursor.execute(
  'INSERT INTO users (name, email, age) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
  ('Alice', 'alice@example.com', 30)
)
conn.commit()
new_id = cursor.lastrowid
print('inserted id:', new_id)

mongoose.definition: Create via new Model(data).save() or Model.create(data) — schema validation runs automatically; hooks (pre/post) can transform data.

topics.title: Reading & Querying
topics.learn: Fetching data with filters and conditions.

sqlite.definition: SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, JOIN and aggregates. Parameterised placeholders keep queries safe.
sqlite.code:
cursor.execute('''
SELECT id, name FROM users
WHERE age >= ? AND city = ?
ORDER BY name LIMIT 10
''', (18, 'Paris'))
rows = cursor.fetchall()

for row in rows:
    print(dict(row))  # Row factory → dict

mongoose.definition: Model.find() with a filter object returns documents; chain .sort(), .limit(), .select() for shaping. Comparisons use $gt/$lt/$in operators.

sqlite.definition: UPDATE/DELETE statements target rows via WHERE — always commit() after writes. Use RETURNING (SQLite 3.35+) to get changed rows back.
sqlite.code:
cursor.execute(
  'UPDATE users SET age = age + 1 WHERE id = ?',
  (user_id,)
)
conn.commit()

# delete
cursor.execute('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?', (user_id,))
conn.commit()

# verify
changes = cursor.rowcount

mongoose.definition: Modify via doc.save() after changing fields, or atomic Model.updateOne/updateMany/findByIdAndUpdate with operators like $set/$inc.

sqlite.definition: Relational joins: FOREIGN KEY links tables; JOIN queries combine them. Normalisation avoids duplication — one source of truth per fact.

mongoose.definition: Two patterns: referencing (store ObjectId, populate() to join) or embedding (nest sub-docs). Choose embed for owned/1-few, reference for large/shared data.

topics.title: SQL CRUD & the WHERE Clause
topics.learn: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE and filtering rows with WHERE.

sqlite.definition: SQL CRUD maps to four statements. WHERE filters rows before the operation — always parameterise values (?) to avoid SQL injection.
sqlite.code:
# INSERT
c.execute('INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES (?, ?)', ('Alice', 30))

# SELECT with WHERE
c.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE age >= ? AND city = ?', (18, 'Paris'))

# UPDATE with WHERE
c.execute('UPDATE users SET age = ? WHERE id = ?', (31, 1))

# DELETE with WHERE
c.execute('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?', (1,))

mongoose.definition: CRUD maps to create/save, find, updateOne/updateMany, deleteOne/deleteMany. Filters are objects — field conditions replace WHERE clauses.

topics.title: ORDER BY, GROUP BY, Aggregates & HAVING
topics.learn: Sorting, grouping rows and computing totals.

sqlite.definition: ORDER BY sorts rows (ASC/DESC); GROUP BY collapses rows per key; aggregates COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX compute per group; HAVING filters groups (WHERE can't see aggregates).

mongoose.definition: Sorting via .sort(), limits via .limit(). Grouping/aggregation uses the pipeline: $match (filter) → $group (aggregate) → $sort/$limit — the GROUP BY/HAVING equivalent.

sqlite.definition: PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row; FOREIGN KEY links a row to another table's PK enforcing referential integrity. JOINs merge related rows at query time.

mongoose.definition: MongoDB has _id (auto PK-like). Relationships use referencing (store ObjectId + ref, join via populate()/$lookup) or embedding (sub-documents). No enforced FK constraints.

topics.title: Constraints & Indexes
topics.learn: Rules on data and fast lookups.

sqlite.definition: Constraints enforce data rules: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, FOREIGN KEY. Indexes (CREATE INDEX) speed up WHERE/JOIN at the cost of write speed and storage.

mongoose.definition: Schema options enforce rules: required, unique, min/max, enum, match (regex), custom validators. Indexes via schema.index() or Model.createIndex() — unique/sparse/TTL/compound.

sqlite.definition: A transaction groups statements so they all succeed or all roll back — critical for transfers (debit+credit). sqlite3 uses isolation_level; commit() persists, rollback() undoes.
sqlite.code:
conn.isolation_level = None  # manual control
try:
    conn.execute('BEGIN')
    conn.execute('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1')
    conn.execute('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2')
    conn.execute('COMMIT')          # both succeed
except Exception:
    conn.execute('ROLLBACK')        # both undone
    raise

mongoose.definition: MongoDB supports multi-document transactions via sessions — startSession(), withTransaction() auto-commits/rolls back. Requires a replica set (Atlas or local rs0).

topics.title: Python → PostgreSQL Connection
topics.learn: Connecting Python to a real Postgres server with psycopg.

sqlite.definition: PostgreSQL is a full client-server DB (unlike file-based SQLite). Python connects via psycopg (v3) or psycopg2 — server runs separately; %s placeholders replace ?. Same SQL mostly.
sqlite.code:
import psycopg

conn = psycopg.connect(
    'postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb'
)
with conn.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > %s', (18,))
    rows = cur.fetchall()
conn.commit()
conn.close()

# SQLAlchemy/ORMs also target Postgres the same way

mongoose.definition: Mongoose connects to MongoDB — locally or MongoDB Atlas (cloud). The connection string holds host, credentials, db name and options; mongoose handles pooling automatically.

sqlite.definition: Pick SQLite/sqlite3 for: small apps, embedded/local-first software, strict schemas, complex JOIN-heavy reporting, zero-infrastructure deployments, ACID guarantees.
sqlite.code:
# Great for:
# - desktop/mobile apps (ships inside the app)
# - prototypes & learning SQL
# - financial/regulated data (ACID)
# - reporting with multi-table joins

# Limit: single writer at a time, no horizontal scale

mongoose.definition: Pick Mongoose/MongoDB for: flexible/evolving schemas, document-shaped data (users, catalogs), rapid iteration, horizontal scaling, JSON-native APIs, high write throughput.
